items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Requested by the researcher. Tree and log: the 1850 census (S1, log_001/log_002) shows Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill; the 1860 census (S2) is cited in the tree but not yet logged. The 1870 census (Ancestry collection 1870 United States Federal Census, paid index, ancestry:7163, Pennsylvania) should show Patrick ~25 either still in Thomas's household or with his own family beside a parent, and neighbors who may be kin. It does not state relationships to the head, so it corroborates rather than proves parentage. Search Flynn with variants Flinn, Flin, Fflynn, Lynn and age 22-28.

The tree cites the 1860 census (S2) for the Thomas-Patrick relationship but no search is logged; confirm the household composition, siblings and the mother's given name from the image. Fills the decade between the logged 1850 find and the 1870 item. Use Flynn/Flinn variants.

Patrick's own death entry (tree: 1908-03-12, Schuylkill, source S3 Pennsylvania Death Certificates, content not yet extracted). The tree gives his birth place as Ireland while the objective says Pennsylvania, and any baptism may not exist or be located (Pennsylvania civil registration only from 1906; Catholic registers sit with the parish, per loc_001). The certificate names the parents and birthplace of the deceased and the informant, a likely relative. Read the image and note that the informant's knowledge is secondary.

Candidate parents' marriage to each other (Thomas Flynn, b. ~1818 Ireland, and his wife). The marriage confirms them as a couple, supplies the wife's name for her maiden surname only if this was her first marriage (not assumed; check for earlier marriages), and its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates the father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Likely a Catholic register (Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, held at the parish per loc_001) or Irish civil/parish records if they married before emigrating; check Irish records if the Ireland birthplace holds.

Patrick's baptism, which names parents directly. Tree says born in Ireland ~1845, objective says Pennsylvania, so test both: Catholic registers of Schuylkill County parishes (diocesan/parish-held; some coal-region church films browse-only per loc_001) and, if Ireland, Irish Catholic registers. Search Flynn/Flinn, Patrick/Patt.

Thomas Flynn b. ~1818 could have died from 1850 to about 1905 (window set by Thomas's lifespan, not Patrick's). The county Register of Wills (from 1811, loc_001) holds wills and administrations naming heirs; a record naming Patrick as son would be direct evidence. Also check Patrick's own estate, 1908, naming siblings and parents.

FAN item: siblings and neighbors from the 1850 household (dwelling 84) and later censuses. Sibling marriages, deaths and baptisms may name the same parents and give a mother's maiden name; neighbors in the 1850/1870 enumeration may be kin or townspeople from the same Irish origin. Also Patrick's own marriage record for his parents' names.

Obituary and cemetery or burial entry for Patrick around 12 March 1908, in local anthracite-region papers and parish cemetery records; these often name surviving siblings, parents' origin and the burial parish, which leads to the church registers.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, cited to a Pennsylvania death certificate, and attaches that source to the Thomas Flynn parent link; the certificate's parent and informant fields have not been read in this project. Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable, and 1908 falls after statewide registration began in 1906 (loc_001). Parents' names and birthplaces on it are secondary information from an informant, so treat as a lead.

Tree cites the 1850 and 1860 censuses for the Patrick-Thomas link, but only as co-residence; the tree gives birth as Ireland ~1845 while the objective says Pennsylvania, so the birthplace needs checking across years. Re-read both households and add 1870 and 1880: the 1880 schedule states relationship to head and parents' birthplaces. Search name variants (Flinn, Flin, Flynn, Floyd) and the household's neighbors.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Catholic registers stay with the Diocese (later Archdiocese) of Philadelphia and are held at the parish (loc_001). Baptism may not exist: if born in Ireland ~1845 no PA register applies, and the birth place itself is disputed, so look for Patrick's baptism, Thomas's family baptisms of siblings, and burial entries.

Patrick's own burial entry after his death 1908-03-12, in the parish or cemetery where he last lived. Because the birth place is unresolved (Ireland per tree, Pennsylvania per objective) and a baptism may not exist, burial and cemetery records may state age, birthplace, and nearby family plots of Thomas or a mother. Cemetery transcription or Find a Grave as lead only.

Patrick's own marriage (church register and county record; Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages are name-searchable; County Marriages begins 1885). Marriage entries may name parents or birthplace. Window starts about age 15 and runs to the end of the collections' coverage for a later marriage.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, per tree, unverified as father) to the candidate mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply her name (if this was her first marriage; a remarriage must not be assumed to give her birth surname), and its date against ~1845 corroborates paternity only indirectly; it does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Marriage may be in Ireland or the US, so check church and civil marriage collections; Irish parish records may require external sites.

Estate of Thomas Flynn at the county Register of Wills (from 1811, loc_001), a primary source naming heirs. Patrick was of Civil War age (about 16-20). Service, draft registration, or pension files (and a widow's pension) may state birthplace, age, and sometimes parents or a dependent mother. Pension files are created after 1865 and testify to earlier events.

| pli_002 | **Parents' marriage, Baiersbronn, 1800–1845** | Marriage entry — gives mother's maiden name | Archion | Names the couple; check for remarriage |

Church books are on Archion (parish page above).

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Birth about 1843, Baiersbronn, Württemberg, no relatives or sources. loc_001 says Baiersbronn Protestant baptism registers are on Archion (paid), not FamilySearch; Germany returned no FamilySearch collections. The baptism entry names father, mother and godparents; read the page by browsing, spelling variants Seeger/Seger/Säger, Katharina/Catharina.

Dedicated parents' marriage item: confirms the couple as a unit, supplies the mother's maiden name (only if it was her first marriage; check for a remarriage), and its date relative to c. 1843 corroborates parentage but does not alone prove Katharina is their child. Candidate couple comes from item 1; the window covers marriages from about 1800 since the parents could be older.

The Familienregister (loc_001) groups parents, all children with birth dates, and deaths on one page; it places Katharina with her parents directly and shows siblings and any remarriage. Search it under the father's name found in items 1-2.

FAN item: baptisms of siblings and the godparents named in the registers, who are often relatives, and the baptisms of Katharina's own children. They name the same parents and test the candidate couple against other Seeger families in the parish.

Subject's own marriage and death or burial entries, as the usual route if the baptism is hard to find or ambiguous. They state age, birthplace and often parents' names. Window runs from her likely marriage age to a late death since she was born c. 1843. Marriage and burial may instead sit in her later parish of residence.

The question's rationale mentions the 1855 Massachusetts State Census, but the tree holds no Massachusetts fact for Katharina, so emigration is an unverified lead. Test it with MyHeritage (the researcher's subscription): marriage, death and census records naming her birthplace and parents, which would say where to look in Württemberg. If nothing ties her to Massachusetts, drop this item.

- The question's rationale cites the 1855 Massachusetts census. Nothing in the tree ties her to Massachusetts, so I treated that as an unverified lead.
- The locality survey (loc_001) says Baiersbronn's Protestant registers are on Archion, a paid site, not FamilySearch. FamilySearch returned no Germany collections for 1800-1930.

**Plan pl_001, in order**
1. pli_001: Baptism register, Baiersbronn, 1841-1845, Archion. It should name the father, mother and godparents.
2. pli_002: The parents' marriage to each other, Baiersbronn, 1800-1845, Archion. It gives the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so check for a remarriage. It does not prove Katharina is their child by itself.
3. pli_003: Familienregister (family register), Baiersbronn, 1800-1900, Archion. It lists parents and all children together.
4. pli_004: Siblings' baptisms and godparents, plus her own children's baptisms, 1830-1860, Archion. This is the FAN item.
5. pli_005: Katharina's own marriage and death or burial entries, 1860-1920, Archion. It is the fallback for pli_001. The baptism may not be findable, and these entries usually state age, birthplace and parents.
6. pli_006: Massachusetts marriage, death and census records, 1850-1920, MyHeritage. It is a fallback for pli_001 and should be dropped if nothing ties her to Massachusetts.

There is no parents' marriage or baptism record on FamilySearch for this place. The first five items are all on Archion, which you have to open yourself, so none can be run through FamilySearch. pli_006 is a MyHeritage search that someone has to run for you.

Hand-back: search-external-sites for pli_001 to pli_006.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Mode:** add-new. The earlier plan for q_001 (pl_002) already had every item completed, and the question is still only "probable". I wrote a new active plan, pl_003.

**Question:** q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**One correction to the request:** the censuses are not all done. The log and the proof summary (ps_001) show only 1850 and 1860 searched. The 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses are still open, so I included them as pli_012.

**What the project already records**
- **Patrick, 1850 census:** age 5, born Ireland, in Thomas Flynn's household (Schuylkill County, dwelling 84).
- **Patrick, 1860 census:** age 15 in Thomas's household (dwelling 112).
- **Patrick's death certificate:** died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County. It names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant was his son-in-law James Brown, so the information is secondary.
- **Birthplace conflict:** c_001 accepted Ireland over the certificate's Pennsylvania. So there is probably no Pennsylvania baptism to find.
- **Thomas Flynn:** tree birth ~1818, Ireland. No death, marriage, wife or probate is recorded.
- **Patrick's marriage:** none recorded.
- **Mother's name:** not recorded anywhere.
- **Timeline gap:** t_001 flags 1860 to 1908 as a high-severity gap.
- **Hints:** no FamilySearch hints item was added. The tree shows no ark for Patrick.

**Plan pl_003, in execution order**
1. **pli_006**, church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: Thomas's burial, 1860-1900. The church collection is name-searchable. The entry may give his age, birthplace and wife.
2. **pli_007**, probate, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: Thomas's will or administration, 1860-1910. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse. The date window follows Thomas's lifespan, not Patrick's.
3. **pli_008**, church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: other Flynn children's baptisms and marriages, and their sponsors (FAN). These could name Thomas and his wife together.
4. **pli_009**, church, Schuylkill County and Ireland (county unknown), FamilySearch: the dedicated marriage of Thomas and Patrick's mother to each other, 1835-1850. It would give her maiden name. It cannot prove parentage alone. It likely took place in Ireland, which has no locality survey yet.
5. **pli_010**, church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: Patrick's own marriage and his children's baptisms, 1865-1895.
6. **pli_011**, church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: Patrick's own burial entry, 1908. This is the subject's own death or burial item, needed because a baptism in an unknown Irish parish is out of reach.
7. **pli_012**, census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: 1870, 1880 and 1900. The 1880 schedule is the first to state relationship to the head.
8. **pli_013**, court, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: Thomas's naturalization, 1840-1900. The anthracite-region films are browse-only. A declaration often names the Irish county of origin.

No item is a fallback for another.

**Needs a locality survey:** the Irish origin place. Once an Irish county or parish turns up, Ireland needs a locality survey before Irish baptism searches are planned.

**Hand-back:** search-records for all eight items, since all are FamilySearch.

It then looks at Patrick's siblings and the church sponsors, the marriage of Thomas and Patrick's mother (which would give her maiden name), and Patrick's own marriage and burial. The censuses are not finished: 1870, 1880 and 1900 remain, and 1880 is the first to state relationships. Last is Thomas's naturalization paper, which may name his home place in Ireland.

Next, the church burial and marriage records and the Schuylkill County probate volumes will be searched in that order, followed by the remaining censuses and the naturalization records.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Feliciana Parish / East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana (1810-1835)

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. This is a geographic split: which successor parish holds a given record depends on where within the old parish the event occurred, and that is frequently unknown. Records for a family resident in the old parish before 1824 may be found under either successor's name after that date — search both.

entry.jurisdiction: East Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
entry.rationale: Marriage registers are the target record. loc_001: the 1824 split of Feliciana Parish was geographic, so the 1828 marriage may sit under either successor; the tree records only birth ~1800 and an 1820 residence in undivided Feliciana Parish, not where in it. Louisiana, East Feliciana Parish Marriage Records, 1824-1900 is name-searchable. Search Bankston with variants (Bankstone, Bankson, Bankstin) and Silas/Silus, 1824-1835 to cover 'circa'.

entry.jurisdiction: West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
entry.rationale: Co-equal with the East Feliciana item, not a fallback: loc_001 says search both successors unless residence is pinned down, and it is not. Louisiana, West Feliciana Parish Marriage Records, 1824-1900 is name-searchable. Same name variants and window.

entry.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
entry.rationale: The tree's only source is the 1820 census (Silas, residence in Feliciana Parish). The 1830 census would show a newly formed household headed by Silas in whichever successor parish he lived, narrowing which parish's registers to read, and age bracket of a wife supports a ~1828 marriage. Search both parishes.

entry.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
entry.rationale: Marriages may be recorded in church registers (Catholic, Protestant) rather than or in addition to the parish civil registers; a church entry may state the place of marriage, and covers the case where the civil registers have a gap or omission. Check the FamilySearch catalog and volume listings for both parishes.

entry.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
entry.rationale: Succession and probate files of Silas, a wife, or her family may name the spouse and place of marriage or her parish of residence. Window is sized to the creators' lifespans (Silas b. ~1800, spouse of similar age), not the 1828 event. Plan as image browse where not name-searchable.

entry.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
entry.rationale: Conveyance and land records place Silas in a specific part of the old parish near 1828 and name neighbors (adjoining owners) and possibly a wife; this identifies which successor parish to prioritize if the marriage indexes miss him. Neighbors and in-laws in these records serve as FAN leads.

---

**Question framing:** Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

**Known context going in:**
- 1870 census: Michael is a farmer, outside Schuylkill County.
- 1882 directory: Michael is a miner in Schuylkill County.
- His brother Patrick bought land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (seven years ahead of Michael), suggesting family ties as well as work may explain the move.

---

**Plan pl_001 — nine items in execution order:**

| # | Type | Record Set / Repository | Purpose |
|---|------|------------------------|---------|
| pli_001 | Census | 1880 US Census, FamilySearch | Was Michael already in Schuylkill County, or elsewhere, just before 1882? |
| pli_002 | Land | Schuylkill Recorder of Deeds, 1875–1900, FamilySearch | Read Patrick's 1875 deed; look for any deed/lease for Michael (a lease may name his mining company) |
| pli_003 | Church | Schuylkill County Church Records, 1865–1900, FamilySearch | Marriage, baptisms, sponsors, origin parish |
| pli_004 | Vital record | Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950, FamilySearch | Civil marriage record with age, birthplace, occupation, parents |
| pli_005 | Census | 1900 US Census, FamilySearch | Did mining remain his occupation? |
| pli_006 | Other | Mining company payrolls & mine inspectors' reports (external repositories) | Directly tests the mining employment hypothesis |
| pli_007 | Newspaper | Local Schuylkill County papers, 1880–1885 (external) | Labor-demand context; may name Michael |
| pli_008 | Probate | Schuylkill County probate, browse, 1875–1940 | Covers Patrick's and the parent's lifespans |
| pli_009 | Naturalization | Coal-region naturalization records, browse, 1860–1882 | Were they immigrants, and from where? |

---

**Next steps:**
- Use **search-records** for pli_001–pli_005, pli_008, pli_009 (FamilySearch, name-searchable or browse).
- Use **search-external-sites** for pli_006 (mining company records) and pli_007 (local newspapers).

The logical starting point is the **1880 census** (pli_001) to establish where Michael was living just before his known arrival in Schuylkill County.

Search Sheahan with variants Shehan, Sheehan, Shean, Sheahen, statewide, not only Schuylkill.

FAN item: the tree records brother Patrick Sheahan buying land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42 p. 118, from James Kelly), seven years before Michael's move, so a family pull may compete with the mining explanation. Read the deed image for witnesses, residence and neighbors, and search the Recorder of Deeds (from 1811) for any deed or lease to or from Michael; loc_001 notes coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so a lease may name his employer.

Schuylkill County Church Records are name-searchable. Per loc_001, Catholic registers stay under the Diocese of Philadelphia and sit at the parish. Look for Michael's marriage, his children's baptisms and sponsors, and any entry naming a prior parish or origin, which would show whether he came from a farm district or via relatives or fellow parishioners. Include Patrick as a sponsor/witness lead.

Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 is name-searchable and covers the years just after the move; a marriage record gives age, birthplace, occupation, and parents' names. Statewide civil birth/death registration only began in 1906 (loc_001), so this is the civil record available in the window.

The 1900 United States Census is name-searchable and records occupation, years married, and for immigrants the year of immigration, plus months unemployed. Employment evidence directly tests the mining hypothesis: coal company payroll and employee ledgers, and Pennsylvania mine inspectors' annual reports (including accident reports naming miners), held by repositories such as the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and state archives. Find the actual holdings and access terms on the repositories' own sites; none is cited here from memory. Not name-searchable on FamilySearch.

Local Schuylkill newspapers of 1880-1885 can show colliery openings, labor demand, strikes and layoffs, and may mention Michael or the Sheahans. This supplies the broad economic context for the claimed mining motive and could name an arrival or employer.

Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse images of the Schuylkill estate files. Wills or estates of Patrick or either brother's relatives may name Michael, his residence and whether kin drew him there. Window runs to 1940 because the creators (Patrick, parent I3) could die decades after 1882.

If the Sheahans were immigrants, a declaration gives origin and arrival year; if native-born, skip. Origin is unverified in the project, so this verifies the starting assumption.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree facts: Michael was resident in Pennsylvania in 1870 (log_001: farmer, outside Schuylkill County) and a miner in Schuylkill County in 1882 (log_002, directory). The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880, name-searchable) falls between those points and records occupation, months unemployed, birthplace, household and relationship to head. If he is already a miner or boarder in 1880 the move predates 1882 and the 'around 1882' premise needs adjusting. Search variants Sheahan/Shehan/Sheehan/Shean/Sheahen.

loc_001: Catholic registers stay with the Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, not the county. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Entries for Michael, a spouse or children and their sponsors can state origin or prior residence; sponsors and witnesses are FAN names (kin or co-workers from his earlier home who may have drawn him to the coal region). Tests the migration cause by revealing who he associated with.

Marriage records (Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950, both name-searchable) for Michael or his children often give occupation and residence. Civil registration of births/deaths began only in 1906 (loc_001), so marriages are the main civil record in the window.

The 1900 census (United States Census, 1900, name-searchable) shows whether he stayed in mining, his years in the county, and children's birthplaces, which date any earlier residence or moves between 1870 and 1900. Covers the later part of the question window.

The Recorder of Deeds holds deeds from 1811 (loc_001). Coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so a purchase by Michael would show he put down roots, and a lease or a deed naming a coal company would link him to the industry. Grantor/grantee indexes are held by the county; locate the holder on the county's own site, as no tool returned contact details.

Local coal-region newspapers and annual state mine inspectors' reports may name Michael as a miner at a specific colliery, in an accident report, strike notice or labor news. This is the nearest available employment evidence, since company payroll records are rarely online. Find holdings via the Historical Society of Schuylkill County or Pennsylvania State Archives sites.

If the 1880 or 1900 census shows foreign birth, naturalization papers (loc_001: coal-region naturalization films can be browse-only, so browse image by image) state residence and date of arrival, helping date his arrival in the county. Conditional on the census findings.

The subject's own death record (Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968, name-searchable) states occupation, birthplace, years of residence and parents. Dated to years after he was last known alive; he may have died before 1906, so check cemetery and burial records in Schuylkill County as the parallel route.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill Register of Wills, not a name search. A will, inventory or petition may name his occupation, heirs and property. Window is set by Michael's own lifespan after the 1882 move.

Here is the research-plan agent's response:

---

**Mode: add-new.** The earlier plan for q_001 (pl_002) was already completed, so a new active plan, **pl_003**, was written. The question is q_001: *"Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"*

---

### What the tree already records
- **1850 census:** Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household (dwelling 84, Schuylkill County). Ancestry's index agrees.
- **1860 census:** Patrick, age 15, again in Thomas Flynn's household.
- **Death certificate:** Patrick died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County; names Thomas Flynn as father; informant was son-in-law James Brown.
- **Thomas Flynn:** born about 1818 in Ireland.
- **Birthplace conflict:** the tree gives Patrick's birth as Ireland, but the question says Pennsylvania. The plan tests both.

---

### pl_003 — Planned items in execution order

| ID | Record / Search | Repository | Purpose |
|----|-----------------|-----------|---------|
| **pli_006** | 1870 census, Schuylkill County | FamilySearch | Shows whether Patrick (~age 25) heads his own household or still lives with Thomas; use spelling variants (Flinn, Flyn, etc.) |
| **pli_007** | 1880 census, Schuylkill County | FamilySearch | First census recording relationship to head and parents' birthplaces — best direct evidence |
| **pli_008** | 1900 census, Schuylkill County | FamilySearch | Last census before Patrick's 1908 death (1890 largely destroyed; 1910 post-death) |
| **pli_009** | Pennsylvania censuses 1870–1900 (fallback) | Ancestry | Fallback for pli_006 and covers any misindexed year |
| **pli_010** | Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother, 1845–1870 | FamilySearch (church registers) | Confirms the couple, names the mother |
| **pli_011** | Patrick's burial / cemetery entry, 1908, Schuylkill County | Cemetery / death records | Subject's own death/burial; Irish birth means no local baptism may exist |
| **pli_012** | Thomas Flynn probate, 1860–1900, Register of Wills | Schuylkill County courthouse | Will or estate papers may name Patrick as a son; also narrows Thomas's death date |
| **pli_013** | Civil War soldiers index & pension records, PA, 1861–1865 | FamilySearch | Bridges the 1860–1870 gap; pension may name a parent |

---

### Next steps
- **pli_006, pli_007, pli_008, pli_013** → hand off to **search-records** (FamilySearch name searches)
- **pli_009** → hand off to **search-external-sites** (Ancestry)
- **pli_010, pli_011, pli_012** → courthouse and parish requests

The 1880 census is the priority, as it is the first to record relationship to head of household. If the free index misses Patrick, the Ancestry fallback (pli_009) covers it.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.
Patrick Flynn age 15 in household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. Consistent with 1850 placement.
Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household in 1850 (age 5, dwelling 84) and 1860 (age 15), and Thomas b. ~1818. By 1870 Patrick (~25) may head his own household or still live with Thomas; either shows whether Thomas (~52) is co-resident. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. 1870 lists no relationships, so infer from age/surname order. Try variants Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Phlynn and Pat/Patk; Irish-born birthplace may be recorded, tree gives Ireland while the question says PA, so test both.

First federal census recording relationship to head and each person's parents' birthplaces, so a Patrick-headed household with Thomas as father or a Thomas-headed household listing Patrick as son would be direct evidence. United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable. Use the same spelling variants; Thomas would be ~62 if alive. Search by household and by neighbors if Patrick has moved within the anthracite region.

Last census before Patrick's 1908 death; records birth month/year, years married, and parents' birthplaces, and shows a widowed father in the household if Thomas lived (~82). United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable. The 1890 census is not planned because it was largely destroyed; no substitute for it is in the tool results. Not extended to 1910 because Patrick died in 1908.

Fallback if FamilySearch indexing misses Patrick under a misspelled surname in 1870, 1880 or 1900; Ancestry's separate transcription may read the Flynn name differently, as the 1850 Ancestry check did for this household. Run only for the census years not resolved above.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) to Patrick's mother, to confirm them as a couple, supply her name (maybe not her first marriage, so no surname is assumed to be maiden), and date the union against Patrick's ~1845 birth. Marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child; the census households above do that. Locality guide: Catholic registers are held at the parish or diocese under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, and no civil marriage registration exists, so plan church marriage registers (parish of residence in 1850) and any Ireland marriage if Thomas arrived married.

Patrick's own burial entry or cemetery record (died 1908-03-12, certificate informant son-in-law James Brown) likely states age and birthplace, and sibling or spouse names. Tree gives birth place Ireland, so the baptism may not be in a Schuylkill register at all, and a Catholic parish burial register and cemetery record are the best route to an origin. Registers are parish-held per locality guide.

FAN and heir evidence: estate or will of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) naming Patrick as son. Window set by Thomas's plausible lifespan (death between the 1860 census and ~1900), not Patrick's. Held by the county Register of Wills from 1811 per locality guide. If no probate exists, his death in the 1870 or 1880 census gap narrows when he died.

Patrick was 16-20 during the Civil War; a name-searchable United States Civil War Soldiers Index entry and pension file could name a parent or dependent mother and place him between 1860 and 1870 censuses. Also bridges the gap between 1860 and 1870 as an intervening link.

agent_returns.text:
Mode: add-new. The earlier plan for q_001 (pl_002) was already completed, so I wrote a new active plan, pl_003. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**What the tree already records**
- **1850 census:** Patrick, age 5, is in Thomas Flynn's household at dwelling 84 in Schuylkill County. Ancestry's index agrees.
- **1860 census:** Patrick, age 15, is again in Thomas Flynn's household.
- **Death certificate:** Patrick died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County. It names Thomas Flynn as father, and the informant was his son-in-law James Brown.
- **Thomas Flynn:** born about 1818 in Ireland.
- **Birthplace conflict:** the tree gives Patrick's birth as Ireland, but the question says Pennsylvania. The plan tests both.
- **Hints review:** I skipped the usual hints review item because the tree has no FamilySearch ark for Patrick.

**pl_003 items, in execution order**
- pli_006: 1870 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Shows whether Patrick, about 25, heads his own household or still lives with Thomas. It is name-searchable, so use spelling variants (Flinn, Flyn and so on).
- pli_007: 1880 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. The first census that records relationship to the head and parents' birthplaces, so it is the best direct evidence.
- pli_008: 1900 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. The last census before Patrick's death. I did not plan 1890 (largely destroyed) or 1910 (he had died).
- pli_009: census fallback on Ancestry, Pennsylvania, 1870-1900. It is the fallback for pli_006 and covers any misindexed census year.
- pli_010: marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother, 1845-1870, FamilySearch. This is the dedicated parents' marriage item. Because Catholic registers are held by the parish or diocese, it is aimed at church marriage registers. It confirms the couple and names the mother. The census households are what link Patrick to them.
- pli_011: Patrick's own burial and cemetery entry, 1908, Schuylkill County. This is the subject's own death or burial item, since an Irish birth means no Schuylkill baptism may exist.
- pli_012: probate for Thomas Flynn, 1860-1900, county Register of Wills. It looks for a will naming Patrick as a son. The window is set by Thomas's lifespan, and it also helps narrow when he died.
- pli_013: Civil War soldiers index and pension records, Pennsylvania, 1861-1865. It bridges the 1860 to 1870 gap and may name a parent.

The FAN requirement (records of associates) is covered by the probate item (pli_012) and the 1870 to 1900 neighbor searches. The first four items and pli_013 are FamilySearch name searches, so the caller should hand off to search-records. The Ancestry fallback (pli_009) goes to search-external-sites, and the church, cemetery and probate items are courthouse and parish requests.

---

I made a new plan to follow Patrick Flynn through the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and look for his father Thomas in his household or nearby. The censuses come first because the 1880 one names each person's relationship to the head of household. The plan then looks for Thomas and Patrick's mother's marriage record, Patrick's burial record, Thomas's will or estate papers, and Civil War records. Birth records may not exist, since the tree says Patrick was born in Ireland. If the free index misses him, the plan includes a second check on Ancestry.

Next, I will search the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County, trying the spelling variants.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Ellen Doyle as a child of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran (Bridget b. ~Ireland 1838); log_002 (1900 census) records 9 children born, 2 living, so roughly 7-8 are undocumented, most likely born in the Doyle marriage that ended before her 1879 marriage to Martin Kearney (log_001). Baptism registers name both parents and are the direct evidence for each child. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable; loc_001 says Catholic registers stay with the Diocese/Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, so search Doyle with Halloran as mother and try variant spellings (Doyl, Doil, Hallorin, Holloran, Bridgit/Biddy).

Dedicated search for the marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran to each other: confirms the couple as a unit, dates the start of the child-bearing window (Bridget b. ~1838, so about 1855-1860), and may name a parish and witnesses. It does not by itself prove any child is theirs; children must come from baptisms or households. Surname Halloran is from Ellen's marriage entry (log_003) and Bridget's 1879 marriage (log_001); treat as unverified until this record is found. Name-searchable church collection; also check the browse-only marriage volume.

The 1860 census (name-searchable) should show the young Doyle household shortly after the marriage, listing early children by name and age. Search John Doyle with a wife Bridget of about 22, born Ireland; use variant spellings of Doyle.

The 1870 census (name-searchable) is likely the fullest picture of the Doyle household with children in the home, including those who died before 1880. Ellen's marriage falls in 1865-1875 (log_003), so she may already be out of the home. Look for neighbors of Irish origin, a mining occupation for John, and children's names to feed the baptism search.

The 1880 census (name-searchable) should find Bridget as wife of Martin Kearney (married 1879, log_001), with Doyle children in the household as stepchildren, whose relationship to the head is shown on the 1880 schedule. Also tells whether John Doyle was dead by then. Search Kearney household and Doyle-surname children under Kearney.

log_002 shows 1900 census says 9 born and 2 living. Identify the second living child (besides Ellen) as an adult in or near the Kearney household or Ellen's household, and check 1910 (name-searchable) for the same fertility columns and for a surviving child living with Bridget. Extends the window to the end of Bridget's life, since later records testify to the earlier births.

Burial entries for John Doyle (died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage, so about 1860-1879) and for Doyle children who died young (7 of 9 did not survive to 1900). Burial entries often state age and parents, and cover children who left no baptism or census trace. Church collection is name-searchable; add cemetery listings for the parish and Find a Grave as a cross-check.

An estate or administration for John Doyle (Register of Wills, per loc_001, from 1811) would name the widow and heirs; a guardianship for minor Doyle children after his death is equally likely. Window is sized to the creators: John's death before 1879, but also Bridget's own estate, which could be as late as the 1920s and would name surviving children. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), as is the county probate volume (image group 007936749, 1851-1930); browse the docket indexes image by image.

FAN item: marriages of the Doyle children. The browse-only county marriage volume (image group 007936753, 1870-1910) and the name-searchable church collection could show a Doyle son or daughter marrying with parents John Doyle and Bridget named, as Ellen's did (log_003). Also re-read Ellen's marriage entry for witnesses, who may be siblings. Civil birth/death registration began only in 1906 (loc_001), so marriage entries are the main civil route.

FAN item: Ellen Doyle's own children's baptisms and her household. Sponsors and godparents are often her siblings or aunts and uncles, and her records may name a surviving brother or sister. Use the name-searchable church collection; Ellen's husband's name comes from her marriage entry (log_003).

Obituaries and death notices for Bridget Kearney and Martin Kearney (Bridget's second marriage, log_001) usually list surviving children and step-children by name, which could name the second living child from log_002. Also notices for a John Doyle death or mining accident before 1879. Check Pennsylvania newspaper archives such as Chronicling America, Newspapers.com or local Pottsville papers.

Deed records (image group 007936752, 1815-1900, partly record-searchable) may show John Doyle or Bridget buying or selling property, with heirs joining in a sale after his death; boundary recitals name neighbors who may be kin. Lower probability, included for breadth.

## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Birth 20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn, with no parents or sources. The Stagstrup church book volume covers 1763-1814, so a baptism naming both parents should exist. loc_001: the register is name-indexed only ~3%, so browse the 1779 images (Denmark, Church Books, collection 2078555 is name-searchable but sparse; image group 004130616 is the browse route) rather than rely on the index. Patronymic Nielsen implies a father named Niels, which is unproved. Record godparents (FAN) and spelling variants Mikkel/Michel/Mikkelsen, Blyeberg/Bleeberg/Blybjerg.

Denmark Military Levying Rolls 1789-1861 (collection 2513529) is name-searchable. Per the Denmark Military Records wiki page and loc_001, boys are listed from birth under their father's name, so the roll is direct parentage evidence and gives the father's farm/residence. Search Mikkel Nielsen born 1779 with variants. Place fields may rank rather than filter, so verify results against the Stagstrup parish.

Fallback if the indexed levy roll search underdelivers: browse-only (personCount 0) image group 004748896, Military Levying Rolls for Vestervig/Thisted Amt districts 1789-1814. Browse the Stagstrup parish section for the 1789-1792 rolls and later three-year rolls, locating Mikkel under his father.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (a Niels and a wife, once named by the baptism or levy roll). It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (patronymic, possibly a prior marriage, so not assumed to be her maiden surname), and its date relative to 1779 corroborates the father. It does not by itself prove Mikkel is their child. The register volume starts 1763, so an earlier marriage may lie in an earlier volume or the bride's parish.

FAN item: baptisms of Mikkel's siblings and the godparents at his own baptism. Siblings baptized to the same Niels and wife test the family unit and reveal the father's residence and kin who stood as sponsors, which helps separate several men named Niels in the parish. Browse image group 004130616.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 (collection 1401625) is name-searchable. The 1787 and 1801 censuses list households by farm with relationships, placing Mikkel (aged 8 and 22) with a Niels and wife, and give the father's age and status to distinguish candidates.

Father's burial entry, needed for the objective's death date. Window runs from Mikkel's birth to about 60 years after, set by the father's plausible lifespan. ## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, sourced to a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), but the project tree has no parents' names from it. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable and 1908 is after statewide registration began (loc_001). Certificates ask for the father's and mother's names and birthplaces, which would test the tree's Thomas Flynn link (R1). Read the image, note informant. Also note conflict: the question says born PA but tree fact F1 says Ireland ~1845.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Replaces pli_006 on superseded pl_002, whose 1870-1890 window assumed Thomas died after 1870; a reference now puts his death around 1865. loc_001 says the county Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811. An estate file naming Patrick among heirs would be direct parentage evidence. Window is set by Thomas's lifespan (death ~1865) with margin; if the Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only (personCount 0) browse the dockets by year, and check a later filing in case the estate was settled late.

Thomas Flynn's own burial entry (death ~1865): St. Mary's Pottsville baptismal registers (S5) already document siblings Mary and James under Thomas, so the parish is the likely burial register. Burial entries often give age, birthplace and spouse, naming the mother. Church registers are held by the parish or Diocese of Philadelphia per loc_001, not the county; also check cemetery records.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 per tree) to Patrick's mother, to confirm them as a couple, supply her name (possibly not her maiden name if she remarried; test by seeking her other marriages) and date the union against Patrick's ~1845 birth. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Tree gives Patrick's birth as Ireland while the question says PA, so also look for an Irish civil/Catholic record via the Ireland collections.

The 1860 census (log_004) put Patrick, 15, in Thomas's household. The 1870 census, after Thomas's death ~1865, should show Patrick with a widowed mother or siblings (Mary, James) or as head of his own household, identifying the mother and testing continuity. Timeline t_001 flags 1860-1908 as a high gap.

Orphans' Court and guardianship records: if Thomas died ~1865 leaving minor children (James, Mary possibly), a guardian petition or estate account names the children and the widow. Tests relationships beyond the probate file; at Schuylkill County Register of Wills/Orphans' Court. FAN: guardians and bondsmen are likely kin.

Thomas's ~1865 death may be war-related and Patrick (~16-20) was of service age: Civil War service, draft registration and any widow's or dependent's pension file can name the soldier's parents or widow. Pension files run decades past the war, so the range is sized to the collection, not to 1860-1870.

FAN item: marriages and baptisms of siblings Mary and James Flynn (and Patrick's own marriage) in Catholic registers, which routinely name parents including the mother's maiden name. Siblings' records speak directly to whether Thomas and the same wife were the parents.

Patrick's own burial and obituary after the 1908 death (certificate, log_005, names Thomas as father, informant son-in-law James Brown). Because Patrick was possibly born in Ireland, before any Pennsylvania baptism could exist, burial and obituary entries may state a birthplace and the mother's name. Informant James Brown's records also fit FAN.
